Public Relations 
Begins 
At Rome 


EDITORIAL 


Nan Vail 


At the beginning of this year we 
start a new chapter in the history of 
Canadian Camping. With the pealing 
of New Year bells we closed the last 
chapter and with the spirit of Christ¬ 
mas still penetrating our thoughts and 
actions, we prepare for the future. 
Christmas cards and messages from 
camping friends across Canada deepen 
that rare spirit of friendship so typical 
of camping people. 

Already hundreds of camp directors 
and their staff members are planning 
for the 1956 camping season. As they 
plan and think, surely somewhere in 
our thought world there is a welding 
together of ideas which will gradually 
gain for us a comprehensive Canadian 
camping philosophy. Our strength for 
the future lies in our combined think¬ 
ing, but each of us has to make our 
contribution. It is giving rather than 
receiving which will build our Camp¬ 
ing Association. 

What have you contributed? Have 
you written or obtained an article for 
our very fine magazine; forwarded sug¬ 
gestions to our National Executive; put 
some real effort into your local organ¬ 
ization? The Canadian camping move¬ 
ment needs the help of every member. 
In December, some board members 
from Toronto and Montreal met in 


our capital city with over 50 camping 
folk from Ottawa, and had a most 
enjoyable experience; such a fine group 
working seriously toward some kind of 
local camping organization. After an 
enjoyable dinner at the Y.M.C.A., we 
had a panel discussion, then broke up 
into five discussion groups. It was a 
worthwhile experience and we appre¬ 
ciated the hospitality. 

To Jack Pearse, “Dusty** Miller and 
the Committee, our thanks and con¬ 
gratulations! The following morning 
the C.C.A. Board met, and a very 
practical session developed under the 
leadership of our President, Irwin Hal- 
adner. We discussed at some length our 
units of organization in an effort to 
find a solution for the problem of 
distance. Perhaps small city units would 
help strengthen the association. A 
National Committee under the chair¬ 
manship of Ted Yard was appointed, 
but he needs the considered thinking 
of all our groups across Canada. We 
spoke with wistful longing of the need 
for government sponsored campsites. 
Canada needs more and more camping 
to give to our young people this unique 
training. 

Camp week came in for some critical 
discussion and we wondered if in the 

conthiued on page 29 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956 


9 



Your Printed 
Promotion .. . 

MAKE IT WORK! 


Every piece of printed matter your 
camp puts out has a bearing on your 
public relations. Printing which is well 
done can contribute much to good 
public relations. Poorly printed mater¬ 
ial can damage public relations. So it 
should be worthwhile to try to deter¬ 
mine how we can make better use of 
printing to improve public relations, 
and how we can refrain from creating 
printed matter which damages our 
reputation. 

There are many different types of 
printed matter which camps do, or 
could, use. Included are picture post¬ 
cards; individually typed personal let¬ 
ters; automatically typed personal let¬ 
ters, mechanically produced pieces in 
letter form; bulletins and announce¬ 
ments; camp newspapers; birthday, 
Christmas, and other special-event 
cards; camp folders, brochures, and 
catalogs; advertising in magazines, 
newspapers, telephone books, etc.; 
articles written for newspapers and 
magazines; and so on. 


Mr. Howard P. Galloway, 

Editor of Camping Magazine, was kind 
enough to present this address at the 1955 
Ontario Camping Association Conference in 
Toronto. Now, for the benefit of those who 
were not able to attend, he has allowed us 
to reprint it in the form of a timely article . 


WHAT’S YOUR PURPOSE? 

Which to use . . . and when . . . 
depends on your answers to several 
other questions. “What are you trying 
to accomplish with the particular piece 
of printing you are currently consider¬ 
ing?” This is a basic question, yet one 


10 


Canadian Camping 




which too often is not completely 
thought through. A good idea is to 
set your primary purpose down on 
paper, in specific rather than general 
terms. If you aren’t satisfied the pur¬ 
pose is clear, concrete and worthwhile, 
start over again. Be sure to get this 
point completely settled before you 
begin actual preparation of the printed 
piece itself. When you do get the 
right purpose down in black and white, 
keep it in front of you as you work, 
to make sure you don’t stray from the 
target. 

Next, get clearly in mind “Who are 
the right people at whom to aim this 
piece?” The best written, best pro¬ 
duced, and best distributed piece of 
printing irl the world, if it is sent to 
the wrong people, will not produce the 
result you want.' So get clearly in 
mind: “For whom am I preparing this 
material?” 

FIRST IMPRESSIONS 
ARE IMPORTANT 

Now it’s time to begin to think about 
actual production of the piece, whether 
it’s a letter, bulletin, booklet, or what¬ 
ever. A good question to start with is 
“What first impression will this piece 
of printed matter make on those who 
receive it?” This calls for consideration 
of the mailing envelope, the design of 
the letterhead, heading of bulletin, 
cover design of booklet, etc.; quality 
of paper; use of colour in paper and/or 
ink; quality of typing or printing and 
other similar factors. 

People get a lot of mail these days. 
Most of it comes in envelopes of one 
sort or another. There are big envel¬ 
opes and little ones, white ones and 
colored ones, all-type envelopes and 
pictorial ones, tastefully done envelopes 


and others in poor taste. No one of 
these can be said to be either “right” 
or “wrong.” It all depends on the type 
of people to whom you are mailing, 
and the type of impression you want 
to create. Your envelope is in com¬ 
petition with all the others and if 
your envelope doesn’t get opened your 
printed piece won’t get read. 

What is important is not whether 
you like the envelope, but whether 
those to whom you mail it will react 
favorably. So consider this (and, as a 
matter of fact, every aspect of every 
printed piece) objectively, from the 
standpoint of the eventual reader. 

The design of your letterhead, the 
heading of a bulletin, or the cover of 
a booklet also need your careful atten¬ 
tion. True, you can scribble some copy 
on a sheet of paper, hand it to a 
printer, and say /‘Print me up some 
letterheads.” If you have a conscien¬ 
tious printer, he will try to pick a 
type and arrangement which he thinks 
will look nice. If his taste happens 
to be the same as yours and the 
readers for whom you are preparing 
your printed material, you’re in luck. 
But make no mistake, it is just plain 
luck. 

A better plan would be to take time 
to think through what design really 
suits your purpose, what printer’s types, 
sizes and arrangement will look well 
in this design, whether any drawings 
or pictures should be included, etc. 
Your printer will be grateful to you 
for supplying specific instructions, and 
the final result will in all probability 
be more effective. Paper and ink are 
two more factors to which careful 
attention is desirable. Paper can be had 
in all sorts of qualities, weights, finishes, 
colors and sizes. Ink comes in a myriad 
range of colors. 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956 


il 


Your budget will to some extent 
control the type of paper you will use. 
So will the method of printing which 
you plan to use. One would not use 
mimeograph paper to print Fortune 
magazine; a fine coated magazine paper 
would produce equally as poor a result 
if used for typing personal letters. 

This is something to talk over with 
your printer. See what he has in stock 
(especially on relatively small jobs, 
using a paper already in stock will 
save you money.) Find out what type 
of paper he feels will reproduce your 
job best. Look over the color range 
of papers available to you; perhaps by 
using a colored paper (which costs 
slightly more) you can get a two-color 
appearance with only one run through 
the press* thus actually cutting costs 
below what would be the result if you 
used white paper and printed in two 
colours. Study samples of the ink 
colors your printer can make available 
to you. If you are using colored paper, 
make sure the ink color will go well 
with the paper. And of course assure 
yourself that both the color of the 
paper and the color or colors of ink are 
appropriate to your purpose and to the 
people who will receive your printed 
matter. 

LOOK FOR QUALITY 
WORKMANSHIP 

Before you contract with anyone to 
do printing for you, check around a bit 
and assure yourself that you will get 
good quality work from the supplier 
you choose. This is important, whether 
you are thinking of a single mimeo¬ 
graphed sheet or a 48-page catalogue. 
There is no reason why, whatever 
method of printing you use, you 
shouldn’t have a quality job. There is 


every reason why you should keep look¬ 
ing until you find a source which will 
give you quality work, if you want your 
printed pieces to be most effective. In¬ 
cidentally, this applies equally as well 
to personally typed letters as to “out¬ 
side printing.” It’s wasteful to design 
and have printed fine letterheads and 
then have them typed on a late 1903 
model typewriter or by an inefficient 
typist. 

Consider next the twin topics of 
format and copy. Which comes first 
is hard to say. Format dictates to some 
extent the amount and type of copy 
to be written. Copv dictates to some 
extent the kind of format to be used. 
But because the form in which the 
material is presented follows so logically 
after the first impressions we’ve been 
talking about, let’s consider format first. 

The format of your printed piece 
should be attractive to look at, simple 
to handle, and easy to read . . . not 
dull and routine. Take some blank 
sheets of paper and cut and fold them 
into what printers call a “dummy” 
of the general size and shape you feel 
would do well for your piece. Sketch 
in approximate location and size of 
the various elements the printed piece 
will contain: headline, photographs or 
drawings, size and kind of type to be 
used, column widths and lengths, and 
so on. Try several different sizes, folds, 
number of pages, and arrangements, 
until you find the one which seems to 
suit best the purpose to which you are 
aiming. 

Watch for these three things: (1) 
The number of pages and kind of 
folding should be such that folding 
can be done by machine. (2) The 
over-all size of the sheet used for 
printing (most jobs are printed flat, 


12 


Canadian Camping 


several pages at once, and then folded 
and trimmed) should be such that your 
printer can use a standard size sheet 
without much left-over waste. (3) The 
finished piece should fit comfortably 
into one of the standard sizes of 
envelopes. 

WRITING THE COPY 

Now, at last, you’re ready to start 
what you wanted to start at the begin- 
ing—writing the “copy” for the piece. 
O.K., let’s go. But keep your primary 
purpose and your rough format in 
front of you, and write the copy so it 
will come somewhere near fitting. Also 
keep in mind that you aren’t com¬ 
pletely bound by the format you’ve 
tentatively chosen. If you get a ter¬ 
rifically better idea en route, there’s 
nothing to stop you from throwing out 
format No. 1 arid starting over again 
with a better one. 

Writing the copy is probably the 
hardest part of the job. What you say 
is important. So is how you say it. 
People may forgive you a somewhat 
less than sparkling format. But, if 
what you say is inaccurate or in poor 
taste, you’re sunk. You need clear, 
careful, and concentrated thinking, self- 
discipline, working and re-working and 
re-working. Remember, the important 
thing is not so much what you want 
to say, but what will impel the reader 
to do what the printed piece is intended 
to accomplish. 

Think objectively as you write your 
copy. Test each word, phrase, sentence, 
paragraph. Is this the best way to say 
it? Will this contribute to the primary 
purpose for which the piece is being 
prepared? Are the headline and lead-in 
paragraph compelling and strong, and 
do they quickly inform the reader what 
benefits will come to him if he takes 
the action you want him to take? 


Does the piece close with a strong bid 
for action? Is the reader told exactly 
what he has to do? 

Is the writing simple, uncomplicated, 
easy to read? Can anything be mis¬ 
construed? Are there words which 
might have another meaning than that 
which you intend? Have you para¬ 
graphed for appearance as well as 
sense? Have you included answers to 
all questions likely to come into the 
reader’s mind? Have you used short, 
easily understandable words, rather than 
long, hard-to-understand words? Have 
you used dramatic, dynamic picture 
words to make your copy “sing?” 

Well, let’s say you have your copy 
written. What do you do now—send 
it to the printer for setting in type? 
Not by a dam sight! 

After you’ve written . . . edit. Then 
edit again. Be your own severest critic. 
Then put your copy away overnight 
and see how it sounds next morning. 
Edit again. Let someone else read 
it—someone who doesn’t know any¬ 
thing more about the subject than do 
the readers for whom you are writing 
. . . someone who won’t polish any 
apples. Get his reaction, then edit once 
more. 

Sound like hard work? It is. But 
it’s worth it in the long run. Why? 
Look at it this way. In ordinary con¬ 
versation cocasionally you may make 
some unfortunate slip or some un¬ 
intended derogatory inference. Maybe 
you’re a little less than clear, or a bit 
long-winded. You can quickly retract 
the slip. Your listener can ask for 
clarification of the unclear part, or 
indicate he’s gotten the point if you 
go on too long. 

But when you put it in print, it’s 
there forever. And you have no way 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956 


13 


under the sun to control who, over a 
long period of time, will read those 
things you’d rather have left unsaid, 
be confused by those things you didn’t 
say clearly enough or misinterpret your 
real point of view. 

Check your spelling, too, and punc¬ 
tuation. Using the dictionary before 
printing is a lot more satisfactory than 
finding out too late that something is 
misspelled. Check again, when you get 
rough proofs from the printer, to make 
sure no errors have crept in during 
typesetting. 

Let’s assume, now, that the copy— 
the written portion of your job—is in 
final and satisfactory form. So back 
we go, and begin to think again about 
format. Is the form you had in mind 
at the beginning still the best? Will 
the copy, as written, fit the space 
sketched in the dummy? 

If the answer to both questions is 
“Yes,” that’s fine. If “No,” you’ll have 
either to develop a new dummy, or 
re-do the copy to whatever extent is 
necessary. Copy that’s too short may 
suggest eliminating a couple of pages 
or so from the dummy, or includ¬ 
ing more “white space.” Most of us, 
including many printers, seem afraid 
of leaving any space unprinted. But 
it can be wonderfully effective, if well 
done. If copy is too long, either it will 
have to be edited again and cut some 
more, or the format revised to provide 
more space. 

The temptation to make long copy 
fit by setting it in smaller type is one 
to be resisted, or at least given most 
careful consideration before a final 
decision is reached. Small, cramped, 
hard-to-read printing may almost com¬ 
pletely ruin the acceptance of your 
finished piece by its recipients. 


HOW SHALL I GET IT PRINTED? 

“What is the best way to produce 
this piece?” is the next question to be 
answered. Let’s discuss the various 
methods somewhat in order of number 
of copies of the material which will be 
required. 

Hand typing is fine, and practically 
the only thing for individual letters 
which must change considerably with 
each person written to. But it’s expen¬ 
sive. 

Where identical or near identical 
copy is to go to a group of people, 
consider automatic typing. Look under 
Duplicating Services in the classified 
telephone book of any sizable city, and 
check the advertisements that mention 
automatic typing. 

With this system every letter is indi¬ 
vidually typed, on your own letterheads. 
But only the name and address, and 
perhaps a few key words which you 
specify, are typewritten by hand. An 
electric device, actuated by a sort of 
player-piano roll, takes over and types 
the rest of the letter without personal 
attention. 

Next in line is the mechanically pro¬ 
duced letter. These can be produced 
either by mimeograph, multigraph, 
multilith, offset printing, or letter-press 
printing. Mimeograph is probably the 
least expensive; multilith or offset, 
which are quite similar, the most 
widely used, and still relatively inex¬ 
pensive. 

These are not really personal letters, 
of course. Usually, however, they are 
printed in type which simulates type¬ 
writing. Sometimes, they are planned 
so that a hand-typed “fill-in” of the 
name and address of the recipient can 
be added. It’s pretty difficult, however, 


14 


Canadian Camping 


to get an absolute match of type and 
color. Most big mailers plan their 
mechanically produced letters for mail¬ 
ing without a fill-in, inserting in its 
place a good strong lead-in sentence, 
sometimes in a second color. Its pur¬ 
pose, of course, is to attract the eye, 
and create desire to read on. 

These mechanically produced letters 
don’t fool anybody, and aren’t really 
intended to. But time and time again, 
test after test made by firms whose 
mailings run into the millions, prove 
that there is some psychological con¬ 
notation of the typewritten letter form 
which makes these “letters” produce 
better results than the same material 
printed with regular printer’s type and 
mailed to the same people. 

Bulletins, announcements, news let¬ 
ters and the like can also be satisfac¬ 
torily produced by mimeograph, multi- 
lith or offset processes. But they must 
be done well, if they are to be effective 
—and too often in camp literature 
their message is largely lost as a result 
of poor production. 

The regular printer’s letterpress pro¬ 
cess can also be used in producing 
materials of this sort, provided the 
printer has a supply of “typewriter” 
type. This method has two potential 
drawbacks: it is likely to be more 
expensive, and it sometimes looks a 
bit too precise and mechanical to give 
the feel of a letter. The second of 
these drawbacks can be somewhat over¬ 
come by using a grayed ink, instead 
of black. 

When it comes to camp folders, 
brochures and catalogs, your choice 
generally lies between letterpress and 
offset printing. Offset is likely to be 
less expensive if you plan for a large 
percentage of the piece to be photo¬ 


graphs; letterpress is likely to be your 
best bet if there is more type matter 
than pictures. 

A growing number of printing estab¬ 
lishments are equipped for both kinds 
of printing, and so can help you choose 
whichever method best suits your cur¬ 
rent need. In some cases, indeed, it 
may prove desirable to use a combina¬ 
tion of letterpress and offset printing. 
In these instances, it would be impera¬ 
tive that your printer have both kinds 
of equipment. Either way you can get 
a result which breathes of a well-set-up 
operation, of stability, of a successful 
camp — provided the piece is well 
designed, carefully written, and capably 
printed. 

Whatever method of reproduction 
you choose, make sure you get a good 
job. Think the printed piece through 
first, before even beginning to write the 
copy. Choose a printer who is known 
for quality work, and for supplying his 
customers with both printing and ideas. 
Any printer can set type and run a 
press. But for really outstanding results 
you need his ideas, too. Work with 
your printer on paper and envelopes. 
Consult with him on type faces and 
inks. Use his talents; on these things 
he is the expert. 

To the degree that you and your 
printer have been able to give con¬ 
sideration to all the factors discussed, 
you will at this point have before you 
a pretty fine piece of printed material 

. designed to fulfil a specific object¬ 
ive . . . written in the very best way 
you know how . . . edited carefully to 
get everything in that ought to be in, 
and everything out that ought to be 
out . . . printed in the manner best 
suited to it . . . and much more certain 
successfully to do the job assigned to it. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956

Soap and Liquid Detergent. Prompt attention given all orders. 

We shall be glad to discuss how we can serve you best. 

Address: Sales Department, Toronto or Peterborough. 

CANADA PACKERS LIMITED 







AMONG 

OURSELVES 


By Jack Passmore 

Associate Professor, 

Ontario College of Education, 
University of Toronto . 

Early one Sunday morning in the 
summer of 1903, several heavily laden 
canoes nosed their way between two 
well-wooded islands in the south-west 
arm of Lake Teinagami. The paddlers 
paused . . . and then leaned forward 
with excitement as the sandy beach 
of a larger island came into view. A 
quick survey increased their mounting 
enthusiasm. Their search was over! 
They stepped ashore and blazed a giant 
pine. This beautifully wooded island 
with its lovely sand beach and protected 
bay was the ideal location for their 
camp. 

Arthur Lewis Cochrane, the leader 
of that camp expedition, was born in 
Birmingham, England, in the year 1870. 
Upon reaching manhood he served with 
the Grenadier Guards for five years. 
But his love of adventure led him to 
Canada in 1894. His all-round athletic 
ability and keen interest in boys resulted 
in his appointment to Upper Canada 
College as physical training instructor. 
During the twenty-seven years he held 



this position, he exercised a great influ¬ 
ence on many young Canadians. 

Camping was a natural outlet for a 
man with so great a love for outdoor 
life. More and more he desired to live 
in the bush and to travel by canoe on 
the lakes and rivers of Northern On¬ 
tario. This ambition caused him to 
establish his first boys’ camp on Lake 
Muskoka in 1900. This is generally 
recorded as the first private camp in 
Canada. 

The canoe trip to Teinagami was 
a real pioneer effort. In those days, 
maps suitable for canoe trip purposes 
were non-existent. Leaving the train 
and the end of steel at North Bay, his 
small party paddled down Trout Lake 
and the Mattawa River to the mighty 
Ottawa. Up the Ottawa river they 
travelled, with frequent portages neces¬ 
sary around enormous log booms. Upon 
reaching the lower part of Lake Temis- 


Toronto , Canada , February , 1956 


17 




kaming, they pushed on to the mouth 
of the Montreal river. (This was the 
same route originally followed by the 
T. and N.O. engineers in the year 
1900). After a difficult and strenuous 
portage around “The Notch”, they 
reached the Matabitchuan. The canoe¬ 
ists then paddled on through Rabbit 
Lake and Snake Lake and, finally, a 
short carry brought them to the North- 
East arm of Lake Temagami. 

Oddly enough, their arrival in Tema¬ 
gami coincided with that of the rail¬ 
road. But modem methods of trans¬ 
portation were still unknown on this 
magnificent waterway. The Hudson’s 
Bay Post had been in existence on Bear 
Island for approximately one hundred 
years. The Cochrane party had the 
thrilling experience of seeing a great 
birch bark canoe, propelled by the 
rhythmic paddles of eight sturdy Ojib- 
way Indians, bringing the Hudson’s 
Bay Factor out to the new railway 
station. 

Because camping was a comparatively 
new venture in Canada, and transporta¬ 
tion difficulties were numerous, Camp 
Temagami grew slowly in the early 
part of the century. But under the 
energetic leadership of its founder, and 
with the devoted help of his wife and 
family, the camp gradually developed. 
Originally the boys came largely from 
Ontario, but eventually the camp 
acquired a well deserved international 
reputation. Among its campers were 
included the sons of many distinguished 
Canadians. 

Today the main camp is still located 
on the original thirty-acre site, but two 
adjoining islands are required to accom¬ 
modate its greatly-expanded pro¬ 
gramme. Excellent accommodation is 
provided for roughly one hundred 
campers. A comparatively recent devel¬ 
opment is a large adult section for the 
use of parents and other guests. At 


the South-East tip of the island over¬ 
looking the open lake, a beautiful 
lodge has been erected. This splendid 
log structure serves as a symbol of 
“A.L.’s” creed in his life-long work 
with boys ... to build slowly but surely, 
so that future generations will benefit 
from his handiwork. 

While many magnificent lake trout 
and other game fish have been landed 
at Camp Temagami, it is the bear 
stories which grip the imagination of 
campers and visitors. The tale of the 
boisterous baby bears is still repeated 
around the dying embers of the camp¬ 
fire, before Lights Out signals the end 
of another camp day. 

Extensive preparations had been 
made to receive Lord Byng, the Gov¬ 
ernor General of Canada. On the 
morning of this important visit, “A.L.” 
awoke in great dismay to find the camp 
a shambles. Two half-grown bear cubs 
that normally delighted the campers 
with their madcap antics, had gone 
destructive. Tents were collapsed, cabin 
roofs slashed, and much other damage 
done. Somehow order was restored 
before the Governor-General and Lady 
Byng arrived. Ironically, the bear cubs 
proved to be one of the camp’s most 
interesting features for His Majesty’s 
representatives. 

In addition to pioneering camping in 
Canada, A. L. Cochrane had a great 
deal to do with stimulating interest in 
skiing. He purchased the first pair of 
skis sold in Toronto, and encouraged 
his boys at Upper Canada College to 
participate in this wondei^ul outdoor 
activity. 

His benevolent influence was also 
cast over the development of swimming 
and water safety. It was he who intro¬ 
duced the Royal Life Saving Society 
programme into this country, and he 

continued on page 43

Canadian Camping 




Bradford G. Sears 

Assistant Professor of Landscape Engineering, 

New York State College of Forestry . 

Consultant Landscape and Recreational Engineer . 


MASTER - PLAN 

YOUR CAMP 


In this period of intenstive planning, 
a strong plea should be made for use 
of Master Plans in connection with the 
development of organized camps. A 
Master Plan 7 portrays by word and 
drawing the ultimate development of a 
campsite, balancing the factors of site, 
topography, capacity, structures, pro¬ 
gram and all the other conditions that 
influence physical layout of the camp. 

It makes no difference whether one 
is working toward a primitive camp or 
a highly developed one. Master planning 
is as essential to selection of an over¬ 
night campsite as it is to location of a 
centralized dining hall. It is as neces¬ 
sary to layout of nature trails as it is 
to location of entrance and service 
roads. It is as interested in control and 
use of springs as it is with development 
of an elaborate water-supply system. 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956 


Hand-to-mouth, day-to-day planning 
will not produce a good camp layout. 
Carefpl thought and study with a long- 
range viewpoint can. The average 
organized camp might well be defined 
as a conglomeration of unrelated struc¬ 
tures unhappily located in an unsuitable 
area. This condition is the result of one 
thing—lack of intelligent planning. 

Planning should begin with selection 
of the campsite. Selection is empha¬ 
sized since the root of evil usually 
begins here. Without factual data to 



19 


prove the point, it is safe to say that 
most organized camps operated by 
public agencies are located on areas 
donated or sold to them for a nominal 
sum for reasons other than the value 
of the area for camping. Many private 
camps are in the same position. Most 
of the subsequent headaches could have 
been avoided if these ‘‘gift horses” had 
been looked squarely in the mouth. 

The list of factors that should be 
considered in the selection of site is 
much too long to include here but 
mention of accessibility, privacy, size of 
area, general elevation, topography, 
forest cover, water features and site 
hazards will give a general picture of 
their nature. 

Upon the site is superimposed the 
Master Plan. Since graphic expression 
is the universal language, this usually 
resolves itself into a series of drafted 
plans showing proposed camp layout 
and the details of design and construc¬ 
tion of each of its facilities. 

The first step must be preparation 
of the General Development Plan. This 
sets forth the location and inter-relation¬ 
ship of all elements to be included in 
the ultimate development of the camp¬ 
site. It should show boundaries of the 
area; its topography, both existing and 
with proposed revisions; location of all 
structures, roads, trails, planting, water 
developments, etc.; in fact, any visible 
object that will assume some importance 
in the operation and program of the 
camp. Liken it, if you will, to an 
aeroplane view of the completed camp¬ 
site. 

It is here the basic value of a 
Master Plan can make itself evident. 
Have you ever built a camp structure, 
be it a dining hall, cabin or wash house, 
in what seemed at the time to be its 
best location, only to find a few years 


later that in the development of the 
camp it had proved to be entirely 
misplaced? Have you ever developed 
a site in one corner of the property 
only to find that in the years of camp 
expansion you have followed the foot¬ 
steps of the man who painted himself 
into a corner of a room? Have you 
ever tried to accommodate 75 persons 
on a site whose saturation point was 
50? These things can be avoided by 
planning. 

A Master Plan can show maximum 
capacity of the site—and it must be 
emphasized that each site has a definite 
maximum which must not be exceeded 
if real value is to be accrued from a 
camping experience. In parks this is 
called “scenic saturation,” a point up 
to which the area can sustain the 
persons using it without any permanent 
harm being done to its character, but 
beyond which permanent harm will 
occur, together with destruction of the 
very features which made the site 
originally so desirable. 

Harmony and simplicity of struc¬ 
tures, together with their individual 
settings, constitute an important visible 
part of a well designed camp. Efficient 
location of all facilities and their rela¬ 
tionship to each other is perhaps not 
so evident to the casual eye, but from 
the standpoint of camp operation 
assumes a position of even greater 
importance. 

Each campsite is an individual prob¬ 
lem of design. There is no standard 
plan that will fit all developments. 
The amount of physical development 
and the correct relation of structures 
to each other must grow from the 
site and from the type of camp pro¬ 
gram that is to be pursued. The 
National Park Service in its publica¬ 
tion “Organized Camp Facilities” offers 
a valuable source of information on 


20 


Canadian Camping 


desirable minimum standards. “Digest 
of Laws affecting Organized Camp¬ 
ing,” by the same Service, is another 
worthwhile reference. Health laws and 
standards of the state in which the 
camp is located will have a direct 
bearing on some features of the lay¬ 
out. 

It should be emphasized that a 
Master Plan is not a rigid, inviolate 
thing. It is a living instrument within 
whose basic framework changes can be 
made to meet changing needs of the 
development it directs. No design is 
ever finished. A little more thought 
can always improve it. Nor is a 
Master Plan a pretty pipe dream to be 
filed away and forgotten. To be 
effective it must work and be worked 
on. 

Master Plan drawings are best sup¬ 
plemented by written documents which 
contain descriptions of conditions and 
reasons for the existence, location and 
design of each feature. Alternatives 
may be suggested and questions raised. 
Type of camp program for which the 
design is fitted may well be outlined. 
Past history of the campsite will often 
prove of value. 

The elaborateness and completeness 
of a Master Plan is somewhat a 
matter of choice. A General Develop¬ 
ment Plan with its supplementary state¬ 
ment is of prime necessity. Beyond 
this would be individual design of all 
facilities shown. Each structure should 
be planned in detail and construction 
drawings made. Details of water supply 
and sewage disposal systems should be 
worked out and presented. 


Plan for Planting 

A planting plan showing arrange¬ 
ment of trees, shrubs and vines on 


the campsite is sometimes indicated, 
especially if much planting needs to 
be done to reclaim abandoned farm 
land. Detailed planting plans for each 
structure are occasionally desirable to 
insure proper blending of buildings 
into their surroundings. Native plant 
materials should be used in all cases. 
Exotic species have no place in an 
organized camp. 

Of great value is a planned order 
of development. For every campsite 
there is a preferable order of construc¬ 
tion of facilities that will best service 
the needs of the camp during its period 
of development. For example, if a 
dining hall is planned, it should cer¬ 
tainly precede a nature lodge or an 
administration building in order of 
construction. However, the dining hall 
must itself be preceded or paralleled 
by construction of water-supply, sewage 
disposal and service-road facilities. 
Those facilities of which there is some 
question as to their actual need in the 
camp plan should be left until last. 
Subsequent development of the camp 
program may prove them superfluous. 


Presentation of Plans 

A word should be said about presenta¬ 
tion of plans. Rough sketches and 
notes written in longhand are as 
capable of producing a good job of 
planning as the most elaborately pre¬ 
pared drawings. The ability of the 
camp planner and sagacity of the per¬ 
sons who carry out its development are 
much more important. Let it be said, 
however, that carefully and attractively 
prepared master plan drawings are a 
distinct advantage. They give an 
impression of careful thought and study 
and are most likely to be given the 
credence of an official document. They 
perform an excellent service in 

continued on page 45 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956

THIS BUSINESS 


Little things count ... in enrolments, in the hiring and keeping of staff, 
in associations with parents, in programme, in administration . . . just as they 
count in everyday life; and in dealing with all people who make your camp, 
it is the small remembrance, the consideration, the thoughtfulness which is 
remembered over the years. 

How good is your public relations? Rate yourself by the check-list below. 
Some of the suggestions are obvious; we follow them, almost take them for 
granted. Some will be new and worthy of trial. All will, we hope, be 
valuable to directors of new camps, and to new directors who have taken over 
camps of long standing. 


Does your camp folder make a good impression? Does it sell your 
camp? Is it presented in good taste? Does it contain full information about 
your camp? . 

Do you avoid (as the plague) use of “high pressure selling” in enroling 
campers? Decision has to come from parents or children. In fact, we know 
of one camp director who talks camping generally on his first visit, without 
mention of his own camp...._ 

Do you make a point of visiting the home of every camper before the 
contract is closed? .. 


Have you tried following up your initial visit with a letter, re-emphasizing 
certain aspects or highlighting items of interest to parent and camper?. □ 

Do you send out a monthly or bi-monthly news letter about camp, 
campers, new improvements to camp site, etc.? .. q 

Have you considered the value of a business reply card or stamped, 
addressed envelope for return of enrolments from former campers?. | | 

Would you consider an Open Week-end at your camp before campers 
arrive, so that parents can visit the camp site and see where their children 
would be living, and to see your dining room, lodges and other facilities? □ 


22 


Canadian Camping 










OF PUBLIC RELATIONS 


Do you encourage parents to visit camp during the camping season? 


Suggest that they do not visit for at least a week after camp has opened, 
but after that make them more than welcome! . 0 

Do you keep in close contact with parents during the camp season, 
through your own letters and reports from counsellors?... 0 

Do you work closely with your counsellors to help them with these 
reports, and to see that illness, if any, is reported to the parent at once?.. 0 

Do you extend invitations to nearby townspeople when your camp 
presents its annual Drama, Circus, Open House or whatever? . 0 

Do you send in a report of such events to newspapers in the camp 

Da you have picture post cards of camp views so that children can 
use them for mailing? ....-._... 0 

What of your mailing list? Is it up-to-date? Are names spelled correctly? 0 

Do you send birthday cards and Christmas cards to your campers and 

Do you invite your staff to an evening of camp movies, the Koda- 
chromes taken last summer, good conversation and good food at your home 
during the winter? -------- 0 

Do you plan your reunion carefully, make it as pleasant as you can, 
give campers and counsellors plenty of opportunity to talk?_ □ 

In your plans for camp buildings have you included a Counsellors* 
Cabin, away from the campers* tents or cabins, where counsellors can laugh, 
talk, sing if they wish, when the days’ duties are over?- 0 

Most important of all, does your budget allow for food in good supply 
for meals, snacks, out-trips and counsellors’ snacks at night?__ 0

We Tried It 
This ye hr 


Dear Parents: 

Your daughter is now safely at camp 
and in the process of getting settled. 
No doubt she will tell you all about it 
in her next letter. We will do our 
best to sec that she is happy while she 
is here. In the meantime here are a 
few suggestions which concern her 
adjustment at camp, and a few items 
of information. 

LETTERS: Your daughter will be 
writing to you every Sunday. Be sure 
that you write to her very frequently. 
Write cheerfully and avoid telling her 
how terribly you miss her, or what a 
wonderful time you are having without 
her. If your daughter writes that she 
is in the infirmary you can feel con¬ 
fident that she is being well looked 
after. If anything serious occurs you 
will hear from us. 

If she writes that she is homesick 
you might quite understandably be 
concerned. Homesickness strikes most 
of us sometime or other during our 
lives. Fortunately not many campers 
are troubled with the disease, (actually 
parents suffer more than children), and 
three or four days usually provide 
sufficient time for recovery. A home¬ 
sick camper is not left alone in her 


(We are indebted to Mr. and Mrs. R. Ray- 
mer, Camp Tanamakoon , for this “letter to 
parents” . . . your Editorial Committee 
invites contributions for this page with a 
view to each of us “gaining through shar¬ 
ing”.) 


cabin feeling sad and deserted. We 
arrange to keep her busy and active 
in her group. It takes a little time for 
anyone to adjust to a new environ¬ 
ment. It is very rarely that homesick¬ 
ness proves to be a lasting or a serious 
handicap. 

If you receive letters which are 
exasperatingly brief it is because the 
writer is too occupied with camp 
affairs to elaborate, but she will tell 
you all about them later. However, 
if you receive letters which worry you, 
do not hesitate to write us to that 
effect. We’ll investigate! 

During the course of this month 
you will receive a letter from your 
daughter’s counsellor reporting on her 
progress at camp. 

PARCELS: Campers love them and 
will ask for them. Feel free to send 
books, wearing apparel, camera film, 
tennis balls, toilet articles, games, 
puzzles, swim fins, swim goggles, quizzle 
books, pocket knives, nature handbooks, 
compasses, flashlight batteries, or any 
suitable camping item. The camp is 
not in sympathy with the effect of 
comic books, love story and confession 
magazines, upon the adolescent and pre¬ 
adolescent mind, nor with the waste of 
time involved in reading them. We ask 


24 


Canadian Camping 


you to bear this in mind when sending 
magazines to camp. One small basket 
of fruit per month is permissible. Our 
storage space is very limited and be¬ 
cause „pf the perishable nature of fruit, 
general distribution is the rule. 

PLEASE , PLEASE , PLEASE DO 
NOT SEND FOOD, CANDY OR 
GUM. In making this annual request 
perhaps it would help if we review 
some of the problems which harry us 
when parcels containing food arrive: 

Should we risk acute indigestion by 
giving the entire contents to the camper 
and letting her eat it all at once? 
Should we give it to her to keep in 
her trunk along with her clothing, to 
nibble at during Rest Hour, after Taps 
at night, or just before her scientifically- 
planned, well-balanced meals? Should 
we let her share it with a few carefully 
chosen friends? Should we ask her to 
be democratic and share it with every¬ 
one in her tribe or in the entire camp? 
If so, when shall we interrupt the pro¬ 
gramme to do this? Should we con¬ 
fiscate it and dole it out to her a little 
at a time? If so, what readily accessible 
filing-system of food storage can we 
devise? Should we, as many camps do, 

: return all such parcels to their donors, 
postage collect? What do we do about 
the disappointment and annoyance of 
the camper whose food parcel is dealt 
with contrary to her dictates? Or the 
camper who receives none? The only 
completely satisfactory solution we have 
devised is a negative one. If no food 
parcels are received there will be no 
problem. 

VISITORS: The camp operates on 
Standard Time during July, Daylight 
Saving Time during August. Generally 
speaking, it is advisable for the parents 
of new campers and young campers 
to postpone their visit until the first 
ten days of camp have elapsed. Also, 
avoid telling your daughter that you 
are coming to visit camp, until your 


plans are definite. If you are afraid 
that she may be away from camp on 
a canoe trip, or picnic, you can inquire 
by telephone. 

The most interesting time to visit is 
at 10 a.m. or 3 p.m. We request, 
however, that you do not plan to arrive, 
or to depart, between the hours of 1.30 
to 3.00 p.m. The entire camp observes 
a much-needed REST HOUR during 
that period; the noise of a water taxi 
disturbs the entire camp. PLEASE DO 
NOT BRING WITH YOU FOOD, 
CANDY OR GUM. 

When you are here your daughter 
may suggest that you take her cabin 
group, or a few friends out to dinner. 
Campers are not permitted to leave 
camp with others than their own 
parents without written consent from 
home. (This necessary regulation pro¬ 
tects unsuspecting parents from a flat¬ 
tering but conceivably overenthusiastic 
estimate of their hospitality) Even a 
half-day’s absence requires a re-adjust¬ 
ment to the group. Therefore, we 
prefer that you arrange to take only 
your own daughter, and that she be 
returned to camp as soon as possible. 
TELEPHONING: We have but one 
line into camp. We are sorry that we 
cannot call campers to the telephone 
during rest hour, nor after 8.30 in the 
evening, nor when they are off in the 
woods or out on the lake. Messages 
about trains, tickets, money, visits, etc. 
will be recorded more accurately if 
given to the secretary or the director, 
rather than to an excited camper. 

The camp is all ready for action. 

A maintenance and kitchen staff is here 
to look after the meals and physical 
set up. But more important is the 
supervisory staff. During the summer 
your daughter’s activities will be guided 
by a staff of thoughtfully, chosen and 
trained counsellors. 

Yours very sincerely, 

— • 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956

Your Canoe 


and 

Your Load 


In the bushland “your canoe is your 
life-line”, and this craft deserves under¬ 
standing and care from its first selection 
throughout its era of usefulness. Over¬ 
loading is only one of the hazards to 
be avoided, and a common one. Struc¬ 
tural weakness and rough usage are 
other dangers. 

There are bark, wood strip, canvas- 
covered wood, metal, fibre glass, ply¬ 
wood and many other types of collap¬ 
sible and sectional canoes, but most 
used, perhaps, is the canvas-covered 
craft. It is the subject of some sugges¬ 
tions by W. J. Stinson, Department 
Safety Officer: 

“When selecting a used, canvas- 
covered canoe, inspect it carefully for 
weaknesses common to this type. Your 
canoe is only as safe as its weakest point. 
Canvas rotted on the bottom or under 
the keel, canvas pulled from under the 
gunwale, broken or cracked keel, ribs, 
planking, thwarts, seats, gunwales, stem, 
paint badly worn below waterline, loose 
patches, ribs replaced by inexperienced 
repairmen, altering the shape of the 
canoe, all lead to danger on the water. 

“To keep the canoe in top condition, 
keep it painted, but remember that 


each coat of paint adds weight. Re¬ 
member, too, that dragging canoes in 
shallow water, on beaches or rocks, 
wears paint off quickly, and the bottom 
may need frequent painting and per¬ 
haps much patching. 

“Don’t spare the varnish on the 
cedar structure inside and don’t scrape 
heavy, hob-nailed boots across the 
canoe’s ribs or set it on rocks or sharp 
objects which might puncture the can¬ 
vas or break ribs or sheathing. Lift the 
canoe well up on shore when not in 
use, making sure that the wind cannot 
roll it over. Leaving it partly in and 
out of the water, especially on a rocky 
shore, may cause serious wear from 
wave action. Empty dirt and sand from 
the canoe frequently so that it will not 
settle between canvas and sheathing 
and cause bumps that will wear through 
quickly. 

“If you have to park your canoe 
overnight at a portage or longer at a 
wilderness camp, remove any trees that 
might fall on it. Keep it upside-down 

“If there are porcupines and bears 
about, wires should be strung from 
trees to support the canoe high off 
the ground and sufficiently far from 


Toronto, Canada, February, 1956 


27 










tree trunks so that ‘Porky* can’t reach 
it. Store the paddles in the canoe or 
within the sleeping area. 

“Wash out the canoe after fishing, 
or the scent will attract bears just as 
the salt in perspiration attracts porcu¬ 
pines. Bears will tear canoes apart 
looking for fish, and porcupines will 
so that a heavy rainstorm will not fill 
it and break its back, 
gnaw gunwales and paddles seeking 
salt. 


“Towing the canoe from shore re¬ 
quires a proper bridle, one that will tie 
down at the end of the keel and give 
a lifting effect. Always carry an extra 
paddle and don’t travel at night with¬ 
out proper lights, especially where 
motor-powered craft are operating.” 

Approximate carrying capacities for 
various sizes and models of canoes are 
given in the following table. Weather 
conditions will govern their application:

continued from page 9 

light of more special “weeks” than can 
be promoted, whether other forms of 
publicity might be developed. There 
are so many subjects to consider and 
your Board cannot plan for the whole 
of Canada. Each province has its own 
ideas; their needs are so varied. If 
each association would do some think¬ 
ing on one topic, how much more 
meaningful the C.C.A. could be! 

Canada is a young country, but 
wields an influence in world affairs out 
of all proportion to her size. In many 
fields today new and different methods 
are being discovered to meet the needs 
of modem living. Can we in camping 
afford to trail behind these groups? 
Our local groups are the important 
units and many individuals put great 
effort into them, but our national asso¬ 
ciation has to speak for Canada, there¬ 
fore we cannot function without support 
from the far-flung posts of our great 
country. 

We live in a great and exciting time 
when we are on the verge of so manv 
new discoveries. Why not in our field 
of camping? We must hold firmlv to 
all that is fine in camping traditions, 
but let us put imagination, creativity 
p nd doin'? into our work. We cannot 
be content with slow transport when 
our modem world demands iet travel. 

There is still much to be discovered 
about camping. Who of all our C.C.A. 
members has the courage and desire 
to help master-mind our future devel¬ 
opment? The Association patiently 
awaits the time when our members 
contribute something of their own 
thinking directly to our national office. 

Our National Board and Executive 
are committed to responsibility for the 
C.C.A. and it is a heavy task, requiring 
much time and thought. They deserve 
the best support we can render. 

Let us make 1956 a memorable year 
in Canadian camping history.

WHAT 

is an Advertisement? 

An advertisement is an attract¬ 
ive piece of literature designed to 
stimulate the sale of goods. 

It should, as far as possible, 
feature a picture of a Naval Com¬ 
mander, preferably one with a 
beard. 

Lots of colour is desirable, and 
encouragement should be given to 
the saving of box tops. 

You Start with a slogan:— 

"I THOUGHT MY TEA 
TOWELS WERE WHITE 
UNTIL I SAW CAMP 
KWA KWAK'S" 

Then you say just what it is 
you are trying to sell 

THE MOST COMPREHEN¬ 
SIVE LINE OF CLEANING 
AND SANITARY SUPPLIES 
FOR SUMMER CAMPS. 

Name any special features of 
your line. 

QUALITY, ECONOMY 
SERVICE REPUTATION. 

And finally, state your name 

KERT MANUFACTURING 

Co. Ltd. 

Easy, isn't it? 

See you at the Royal York.

Canadian Camping 







An Appreciation by 
Dorothy M. Douglas 


Under Open Sms 


The dedication of Mary Edgar’s new 
collection of chapel talks and poems 
reads “To Campers Everywhere.” Be¬ 
neath it my imagination has written in 
the lines of William Blake 

1 will give you a golden string; 

Only wind it into a bally 

It will lead you to Heaven’s Gate 

Built in Jerusalem Wall. 

With her two books, WOODFIRE 
• AND CANDLELIGHT (a collection 
of her poems) and now UNDER 
OPEN SKIES (Clarke, Irwin & Com¬ 
pany Ltd., Toronto ($2.50) she gives to 
campers and counsellors everywhere 
iust such a golden string to wind. 
Fashioned not of light cotton string, 
or coarse hemp cord, nor yet of dainty 
satin ribbon, it is a string of the finest 
materials, its strands strong and shining, 
strong with a great conviction, and 
shining with the radiance of faith. It 
is a string that vibrates with music 
too—the music of poetry. 

What camper does not love to be 
told a story? Jesus, the greatest 
Teacher of all, chose the parable or 
story through which to tell His listeners 
about God and the crood fife. Tobn 
Bunyan in PILGRIM’S PROGRESS 
described the life of a Christian as the 
ioumey of one particular man. Mary 
Edgar is also a wonderful narrator, 
telling her story or poem with magnetic 
warmth and sincerity. She knows that 
it is difficult for children to find signi¬ 
ficance in abstract concepts: courage, 
honesty, kindness, valour. And so she 
chooses the story that stirs their imag¬ 
ination, or the poem that paints a 
picture of something they too have 


seen. To those who have attended 
Glen Bernard Camp since she founded 
it 33 years ago, her Sunday morning 
. services in the high outdoor chapel 
have been a great source of inspiration. 
It. is good to know that something of 
this experience can now be shared with 
the readers of her books. 

As a camp director or counsellor, 
you are probably asked from time to 
time to help in planning a worship 
service or to give an inspirational talk. 
UNDER OPEN SKIES will be a great 
help to you. The tales she tells of The 
Bell of Kiyomizu, A Jaipur Rug, The 
Cryptomeria Trees of the Tokaido 
Road. The Chinese Rickshaw Boy and 
the Embroidered Slippers are sheer 
romance. There is the legend shared 
with Glen Bernard by Dawendine, 
daughter of a Chief of the Mohawks. 
There are talks inspired by events of 
the day, incidents from the Bible, 
moments of beauty in the out-of-doors. 
Finally, there are some of her loveliest 
poems and prayers, and a few by such 
other well-known writers as Mary L. 
Northway, which may be read as they 
are, or which may inspire you with 
some thought that you can express in 
your own words. 

One of the strongest strands in the 
string Mary Edgar places in her read¬ 
er’s hand is her conviction that to 
those of us who seek Him, God will 
reveal His Presence and His purpose 
for us (“His lamps are we, to shine 
where He has need”), and that there 
is no surer place to find Him than in 
the midst of His handiwork—under 
open skies! 

—• 


Toronto , Canada, February } 1956

National News & Notes 


Whenever and wherever camping 
people from all parts of Canada are 
gathered together, always the thought 
is expressed: “If only members from 
the West Coast, from the Prairies and 
from the Maritimes could be with us.” 
That same wish echoed around the 
conference table in the Terrace Room 
at the Chateau Laurier. If only repre¬ 
sentatives could be on hand to complete 
the whole camping picture as situations 
come to light and discussions arise. It 
is our fond hope, now, that C.C.A. 
members from far-away points might 
be in Toronto on business when we 
gather for the Annual C.C.A. Meeting 
at the Royal York Hotel on the even¬ 
ing of March first. Keep it in mind. 
Join us if you can possibly do so. A 
rousing welcome will be extended. 

One of the interesting decisions to 
come out of the Ottawa Board meeting 
is that concerning a History of Can¬ 
adian Camping. The plan is to involve 
as many as possible of our Elder 
Statesmen in the camping world, by 
asking them to contribute some of their 
experiences and other information 
about their own camp development 
which was that very history in the 
making. The idea is developing. One 
day we will have a documented report. 
How colourful it will be! 


The YWCA Annual Meeting in 
Toronto sparkled with ideas and dis¬ 
cussions and purpose, but for one-half 
hour an audience sat in complete ad¬ 
miration of Mary Barker’s new 8 mm. 
film, two reels long and realistic in 
colour, taken last summer on a tour 


of some of the YWCA camps across 
Canada. 

Film party leaves from Camp Tapa- 
wingo, the Toronto camp at Parry 
Sound, and goes on to Camp Kinnaird 
in its magnificent Lake of the Woods 
setting, operated by the Winnipeg 
YWCA. Calgary and Edmonton camps 
take up a portion of the second reel 
which is completed with views of 
Georgian Bay from London’s Camp 
Queen Elizabeth, views reminiscent of 
Tom Thomson and Arthur Lismer. 

Camping people wishing to borrow 
the film may do so . . . but borrow it 
as they would London Tower’s Crown 
Jewels. This is a one-of-a-kind produc¬ 
tion. The film’s irreplaceable. So, 
write to Miss Mary Barker, YWCA of 
Canada, 571 Jarvis Street, Toronto 5, 
Ontario. It’s that precious it’s sent 
out by registered mail only, and must 
be returned the same way. 


Chuck Roche, Director of Public 
Relations for the B.C. Camping Asso¬ 
ciation, keeps us well informed on the 
doings of that Province. A recent News 
Letter says: “Camping is to be in¬ 
cluded in the area recreation of the 
B.C. Natural Resources Conference. 
This Conference, which is made up 
Government, Industry and University, 
meets once each year to receive reports 
on all aspects of B.C.’s resources, and. 
if desired, to advise the Government 
on these reports. This Association has 
been asked to prepare a brief on Camp¬ 
ing in B.C. The past, present and future 
activities and requirements of the Asso¬ 
ciation, as well as the camping move¬ 
ment as a whole, are to be covered.”

Canadian Camping 


News from Alberta is that the Camp¬ 
ing group in their province is to 
approach the Provincial Government to 
rescind taxes on camp land. 

“As a result of the first Annual Con¬ 
ference of the Alberta Camping Asso¬ 
ciation there is now a move on foot from 
this group to have a bill introduced 
in the Provincial Legislature in 1956 
to have taxation rescinded on camp 
property where the camp is operating 
on a non-profit-making basis. Some 
camps, such as the Church and the 
Y.W.C.A. pay as much as $100.00 a 
year in taxation on camp property, and 
we have every reason to believe that 
a bill to remove this taxation will be 
passed in the Legislative Assembly. 
Combined with the taxation appeal, 
the Alberta Camping Association hopes 
to strengthen its membership and have 
all camps in the province represented 
in its activities. The uniting behind 
this taxation appeal indicates what can 
be done when camping combines its 
voice for a just cause. Many of us 
realize how slim a budget agency and 
similar camps are operated on. Should 
taxation be removed, these particular 
camps would benefit. Interestingly 
enough, this appeal will be backed by 
all camps, even by those who do not 
pay camp taxation to the Province, 
but who are lending financial assistance 
for the presentation of the bill.** 

The Alberta Camping group is also 
considering, as one of its projects for 
this vear, the writing of a generalized 
booklet on Standards as it affects 
Personnel. 


From the Mari times comes a hint of 
another Open Meeting in Halifax to¬ 
wards the end of February, with a key 
speaker who will conduct a question- 
and-answer period for the balance of 


the evening. Camping folk everywhere 
appreciate the type of meeting which 
fosters the free exchange of ideas; so 
we will be interested to hear the final 
plans. 

Our sympathy to Maritimers goes 
out at this stormy time as nature takes 
her toll. While damage is reported to 
be widespread, we hope camp sites 
remained intact, so that campers can 
enjoy the best summer ever. 


President of the Regina YWCA, Mrs. 
L. B. Thomson, and Executive Director 
Miss Isabel Russell, graced our portals 
to intrigue us with talk of “prairie 
camping, its joys and problems,” as 
refreshing as the first breeze of a 
prairie summer. Our best wishes to 
them in a project we hope we’ll soon 
be given the All Clear to write about 
in detail. 


The Honourable Isabel Catto, new 
World President of the YWCA, visited 
Toronto to speak at their Annual Meet¬ 
ing banquet, but found time to talk with 
us, for a few pleasant moments, of her 
deep interest in camping, and her desire 
to know more about how we do it in 
Canada. A speaker with the purest 
diction we’ve heard in a long time, 
her dinner address brought to her 
audience something of her daring work 
during war years, in all parts of the 
world, under Lady Reading, Viscountess 
Mountbatten and Lady Churchill. She 
brings to the YWCA a wealth of 
experience, a knowledge of the needs 
of people under stress and in time of 
peace, a kindly tolerance and a strength 
of purpose, the value of which will 
surely leave its mark on the history of 
that worthy organization.

New Zealand sent us a visitor just 
before the close of the year. Professor 
Philip A. Smithells, Director, School of 
Physical Education, University of 
Otago, at Dunedin, travelled around 
the world in the interest of Physical 
Education research. Professor Smithells 
firmly believes that camping and Physi¬ 
cal Education go hand-in-hand. Too 
short a visit to National Office sent him 
on his way with a little of the informa¬ 
tion he wanted, plus a handful of names 
and addresses . . . camping people in 
Canada and the United States who, 
we know, are walking encyclopaedias 
on the subject. Incidentally, if you’re 
thinking of going Down Under for 
canoeing, ’s no use! It’s unknown! 
Rivers too swift; lakes like inland seas, 
too big; no canoeing country such as 
our Canadian north provides. 


“It’s always fair weather . . . and 
good friends did get together, if only 
for a short time, at the Ottawa CCA 
Board Meeting. *Twas gay indeed to 
catch up on all the news with Agnes 
Mutchler, Ken Murray and Nan Vail 
who is receiving congratulations on her 
appointment as Executive Director of 
the St. Laurent Neighbourhood Asso¬ 
ciation in Montreal. We know Jack 
Pearse is always glad to see C. B. 
Stafford of the National Boy Scouts 
Association, and at this meeting we 
were pleased to meet P. J. Horan of 
the same Association, and to share 
his views on safety and standards. 


We wonder if all our readers know 
of the honours shared by Miss Mary 
Edgar and the YWCA. For the recent 
Annual Meeting in Toronto, Miss 
Edgar wrote a special hymn for the 


34 


Canadian Camping 




occasion, which was sung at the closing 
Service of Dedication at Convocation 
Hall with the Mendelssohn Choir, 
under the direction of Sir Ernest Mac¬ 
Millan. As delegates and guests crossed 
the campus on the way to Hart House 
to tea, the bells of the carillon pealed 
out the hymn’s tune, and it made us 
very proud to know its author is a 
member of our Executive. Almost like 
having a Poet Laureate with us, isn’t 
it? 


THE EDITOR’S GUESTS . . . with 
a great deal of pleasure and apprecia¬ 
tion we welcome NAN VAIL as the 
author of a timely Editorial for this 
issue ... as soon as we were told 
JACK PASSMORE would write about 
Mr. A. L. Cochrane for Among Our¬

courage, ingenuity, humour and intel¬

Although he takes no credit, it was 
the Ontario Department of Lands and 
Forest’s “BILL” STINSON who dis¬ 
covered the need for canoe capacity 
loads, and who sat down and figured 
them out ... For a long time we have 
wanted to run BRADFORD SEAR’S 
article on the camp plan, for the benefit 
of new camp directors . . To ELIZA¬ 
BETH WARDLEY RAYMER, many 
thanks for an excellent letter to parents 
which will, no doubt, be adapted for 
use in many camps . . . and to DOR¬ 
OTHY DOUGLAS who writes so easily 
and informatively of our new books, 
and who travels from Oakville to Tor¬ 
onto to attend a good percentage of 
our meetings, Thank You seems hardly 
enough!

There is a young dictaphone typist 
working in New York City’s Welfare 
Department. After hours, she is also 
the co-leader of a Girl Scout Troop. 

What’s so unusual? One, she is 
blind. Two, she has been a Girl Scout 
continuously for 20 years. Three, she 
is the co-leader of a blind Girl Scout 
troop in the same blind school which 
she attended as a child and young girl. 
Four, her mother is the leader. Five, 
she is the reason her mother, with sight, 
is a Girl Scout leader for these blind 
girls. Two of the girls in the troop 
are twins, blind from birth. 


Out of the Mail Bag on Press Day 
comes a note from Vernon McAdam 
of the Boys’ Clubs of Canada in Mon¬ 
treal. You will remember our review 
of Mr. McAdams* inspiring book. 
Twenty Twenty-Minute Talks to Boys, 
in the December, 1954 issue. The book 
is available without charge and, as 
might be expected, the first printmg 
ran out almost immediately. The 
second printing is now ready, so if you 
were disappointed last year, send in 
your name now. The address: Boys’ 
Clubs of Canada, 6 Weredale Park, 
Montreal 6, Quebec.

by Dorothy M. Douglas 


TRACKS, TRAILS AND SIGNS 

Fred J. Speakman 

To anyone who does not actually see 
an animal or a few birds in a stretch 
of field or woodland, it might seem that 
no creatures frequented the place. Yet 
fields and hedges are full of animals 
and their homes which we can discover 
if we know where to look. TRACKS, 
TRAILS AND SIGNS is not a natural 
history book, but rather a book that 
makes the reader want to get outdoors 
to look, smell, hear, and see things for 
himself. The author states “I should 
like to show you how to look and then 
to set you on the right road to under¬ 
standing something of what you see 
and hear.” 

The best way to learn is by watching 
and stalking. Simple signs sometimes 
present fascinating stories to unravel. 
The dropped feather, the tuft of hair 
or fur on a -barbed wire fence, a few 
wood chips, tunnels in the grass, holes 
in the trees, droppings, tracks, all are 
exciting bits of evidence that creatures 
are about. No wonder we rarely see 
them. A deer’s sense of smell is so 
acute that he can smell you half a 
mile away if the wind blows from you 
to him. If you are standing motionless 
20 feet from a badger you have only 
to swallow and he will dash under¬ 
ground. 

There are lots of helpful tips about 
tracking wild animals. For instance, 


did you know that to find tracks best 
you should go with the sun in your 
eyes and when long shadows lie across 
the fields; the tracks will show up light 
with black edges. After dark, carry 
your flashlight low and level with the 
ground. The book is generously illus¬ 
trated with drawings a child could 
trace. While written about the wild 
life and conditions that prevail in Eng¬ 
land, particularly in Epping Forest, 
this book has more to offer the Can¬ 
adian reader than I expected to find. 
As the writer observes, “Certain facts 
and principles remain true everywhere.” 
Clarke, Irwin & Company Ltd., Tor¬ 
onto. $2.10. 


FLOWERS—A Golden Nature Guide 

A sturdy little pocket-size book de¬ 
signed for easy reference on the trail, 
this is one of a series which includes 
Birds, Insects, Trees, Stars, Reptiles 
and Amphibians, all written by eminent 
authorities under the sponsorship of 
The Wildlife Management Institute of 
the U.S.A. Here are 134 full-colour 
pictures of wild flowers, arranged in 
four groups according to colour, having 
coloured tips on the pages to indicate 
these sections. A page is devoted to 
each flower, giving a 60 to 70 word 
description and a miniature diagram of 
the area in the U.S.A. where it may 
be found. It is striking to note how

AUTO CAMPERS’ 

GUIDE TO CANADA 

George and Iris Wells 

An urge to see the country and to 
visit new places informally, to try the 
simple outdoor life with tent and cook- 
stove has a great appeal for the former 
camper or counsellor. One has only 
to travel a highway, and picnic at a 
public campsite to observe how many 
people have taken to the idea of a 
holiday camping trip by car. Not every¬ 
one has a summer cottage, nor the 
budget for a resort holiday, but nearly 
every family has a car. 

The Wells offer a guide to all the 
public and private lands available to 
the auto camper in Canada. Over 
1,000 campgrounds are recorded here, 
grouped by province and highway num¬ 
ber for easy reference. A directory of the 
hotels, lodges, and cabin camps oper¬ 
ated by the government or under con¬ 
cession on public lands. It is impressive 
to realize how many national and prov¬ 
incial parks and areas of crown land 
in Canada, still in their natural and 
unexploited state, are accessible by 
good roads and open to campers who 
register suitably on entering them. 

Chapters on planning a trip, suggest¬ 
ing equipment, tenting techniques, trail¬ 
er camping, and what kind of scenery 
and general conditions await you in 
each part of the country contribute to 


38 


Canadian Camping 




making this an excellent handbook. 
Having heard how much fun was had 
by a brother, his wife and four young 
children on a camping trip in their 
Morris Oxford car with a tourist tent, 
a pup tent, and 6 sleeping bags strapped 
in a play pen on the roof, we recom¬ 
mend such an outing to all the young 
and adventurous, and with a few more 
comforts added, to even the uninitiated. 
Musson Book Co. Ltd., Toronto. $3.00. 

THE UNESCO COURIER 

Published monthly at United Nations, 

New York City 

“A window open on the world” is 
the sub-heading on this official organ 
of the United Nations Educational and 


Cultural Organization. Generously il¬ 
lustrated and prepared with the best 
American magazine techniques, this is 
a very fascinating publication which 
would be well-thumbed if placed in 
your senior campers’ or counsellors’ 
lounge or reading centre. 

For instance, the December 1955 issue 
contains an illustrated letter entitled 
DEAR JENNY from a father to his 
15-year old daughter, in which he tells 
her about what the United Nations is, 
and how it goes about its great task. 
He sympathizes with the fact that at 
her age, reading the news is a little 
like walking into a movie after the 
film has been running for an hour—

everyone is rushing about but it is not 
clear who is going where and why. 

The idealism and enterprise of young 
people disposes them to respond en¬ 
thusiastically to the dream of world 
peace and brotherhood which is the 
aim of the United Nations. Because 
in Canada we have such a high 
standard of living, such infinite natural 
resources, we can easily grow up ignor¬ 
ant or indifferent to the great needs 
of other lands. Through the UNESCO 
COURIER’S articles and pictures we 
can become better informed about the 
state of the world, and become aware 
of the opportunities there are for each 
person to take an active part in the 
building of a better community, a 
better country, a better world. Sub¬ 
scription $2.50 a year; 25c a copy, 
sent to UNESCO Publications Center, 
475 Fifth Avenue, New York 17. 


CANADIAN YESTERDAYS 

Edgar A. Collard 

For a book that combines history 
with the light sort of reading one 
prefers for the summer, no better choice 
than Canadian Yesterdays has come 
to hand for a long time. While most 
of the anecdotes are centered in Lower 
Canada, notably Montreal, Quebec, and 
the Maritimes, all have a bearing on, 
Canadian history, and centre about 
names we all know and with whose 
descendents many of us are acquainted: 
the Monk family and Monklands in 
Montreal; Captain Matthew Webb: 
Dr. Wilfred Grenfell of Labrador; Lord 
Strathcona; Reverend James McGreg¬ 
or; Bishop Mountain; Thomas D’Arcy 
McGee; the famous Little Doctor, Dr. 
George Dawson, explorer and Dominion 
Surveyor who gave his name to Dawson 
City. 

The glimpse we are given of Lady 
Macdonald, wife of Sir John A., cross- 


40 


Canadian Camping 





ing the Rockies on the cowcatcher of 
a railway engine, of Charles Kingsley 
speaking in Toronto and Montreal, of 
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle and his deep 
love for Canada, refresh the reader and 
give insight to the customs and thoughts 
of an era far agone. 

A camp library should hold more 
books of this sort for older campers 
and those of the staff who take Can¬ 
adian History seriously and prefer it 
in pleasant doses. Longmans, Green 
and Company, Toronto 16—$4.50. 

—E.F. 

THE STRUGGLE 
FOR THE BORDER 

Bruce Hutchison 

In the words of the author in an 
Introduction to his latest book: “This 
is not a formal book of history. It is 
an adventure story of men in action 
and careless of what history would 
record.” He has no way of knowing, 
however, how full of adventure his writ¬ 
ing is, for actually he has created much 
of Gilbert Parker’s colourful action and 
some of the glamour James Oliver 
Curwood gave to The Plains of Abra¬ 
ham; excitement leads one from page 
to page, from chapter to chapter to the 
end of a book truly Canadian, written 
through Canadian eyes. 

From 1535 to 1955, Mr. Hutchison 
traces North American development as 
it is related to the rest of the world, 
and shows from time to time how 
precarious was our position and how 
near we came to extinction as a Nation. 
“It deals with people,V he goes on to 
say, “many of them quite irrational. 
iThe writer’s modest purpose will be 
served, therefore, iLsuch a tale interests 
the reader in the past and future 
affairs of America, which, he believes, 
liare greatly misunderstood and in urgent 
need of understanding.” Longmans, 
Green and Companv, Toronto 16— 
$6.00. ' —E.F.

continued fro?n page 18 

has been closely identified with it ever 
since. Approximately ten years ago, 
when the Canadian Red Cross Society 
decided to include water safety in its 
peace-time programme, “A.L.’s” counsel 
and guidance were sought, and he still 
remains an active member of that 
organization. 

Through the years, much public 
recognition has come his way. He was 
one of the founders of the Canadian 
Camping Association, and has been its 
Honorary President for many years. He 
is also Honorary President of the 
Ontario Camping Asociation, and one 
of the most valued advisers on its 
Board. 

In 1907, he received the highest 
recognition possible in the life saving 
field. For distinguished service to the 
Royal Life Saving Society, King 
Edward VII appointed him an Honor¬ 
ary Associate of the Hospital of St. 
John of Jerusalem. To commemorate 
the fiftieth anniversary of his camp 
in 1949, the Honorable Dana Porter, 
then Minister of Education for Ontario, 
presented him with a memorial plaque. 

But the greatest possible tribute to 
the esteem in which A. L. Cochrane 
is held, came in November, 1954. 
Approximately one hundred close 
friends and well-wishers attended a 
testimonial dinner held in his honour. 
“A.L.” was lauded by dozens of Can¬ 
adian citizens, prominent in every walk 
of life. Sometime during his active 
camping career they had all felt the 
impact of his high ideals, manly 
courtesy, and kindly philosophy. 

When the story of Camping in 
Canada is eventually written, one 
important chapter will deal with the 
vision, inspiration and example of 
Arthur Lewis Cochrane.

The River "Pointer” 

C. R. Blackstock, 

Director, Camp Mazinaw , 

Two summers ago we were able to 
get a couple of “pointers”, or river 
boats, built by a local craftsman. We 
had an old one upon which to model 
the new ones. 

These craft are some twenty-four 
feet in over-all length. When used by 
lumbermen for driving logs they are 
equipped with sweeps or oars. We did 
not have oar-locks put on ours as it 
was planned to paddle them. 

Eight to ten boys, depending upon 
their size, can use a pointer safely, 
moving it along at a good speed. For 
tripping around larger lakes they are 
ideal since they are so seaworthy. A 
short mast for a square sail can be 
rigged on them for running before the 
wind. 

We have found them ideal for teach¬ 
ing paddling, especially to smaller 
campers. Stroke rhythm, keeping in 
stroke with others, and the basic strokes 
—forward, backward, and draw—can 
be practised on the water in a craft 
that permits one instructor to help a 
group rather than just one camper at 
a time. 

Perhaps the most interesting feature 
about these picturesque Canadian 
watercraft is that, they can be con¬ 
verted so easily to a pirate ship, a 
viking vessel, or some other glamorous 
vessel of the young’s imaginative inven¬ 
tion. 

Having a pair of them permits their 
use in regattas, too. Well paddled, the 
pointers make a colourful addition to 
the events. 

We recommend the pointer as a craft 
for summer camps. They are steady, 
safe, and dependable. They can be 
constructed of native woods in a very 
durable fashion. 

—•
